question_record.context: A suspicious PowerShell activity was observed on the machine which might indicate usage of PowerShell during installation, exploration, or lateral movement activities by attackers. Attackers often use PowerShell to bypass security protection mechanisms by executing their payload in memory without leaving any trace. As part of this activity, the process `winword.exe` executed a file `winatp-intro-backdoor.exe`. Subsequently, Task Scheduler activity was noted, which might involve malicious code being launched automatically to establish persistence.
question_record.question: What is the Security Identifier (SID) of the account that performed the suspicious Task Scheduler activity?
solution: A suspicious PowerShell command line was executed using the process `powershell.exe`.
The user with SID `S-1-5-21-1870156660-7534030218-135086563-1193` used Task Scheduler in a suspicious manner, likely attempting to establish persistence by creating, modifying, or deleting a task.

10.name: Suspicious PowerShell command line
10.description:
A suspicious PowerShell activity was observed on the machine. 
This behavior may indicate that PowerShell was used during installation, exploration, or in some cases in lateral movement activities which are used by attackers to invoke modules, download external payloads, or get more information about the system. Attackers usually use PowerShell to bypass security protection mechanisms by executing their payload in memory without touching the disk and leaving any trace.

21.name: Suspicious Task Scheduler activity
21.description:
A process involved in earlier malicious activity used Task Scheduler to create, modify, or delete a task. This might be an attempt launch malicious code automatically and establish persistence.

For further information on this threat, read the following threat analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/c9709a39-ac8d-493d-9a63-71da3ca1e745/analystreport

interpretation.scope: official graph witness, not a proof of causality, actor identity or autonomous planning

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.AlertId, o.AlertTitle, o.ObservedAt, o.EntityIndex,
       o.GraphValue AS value, o.RawComponents, o.Roles, o.SourceRowHash,
       i.GraphValue AS matched_input
FROM LTMInputEvidence i
JOIN LTMEntityEvidence o ON o.SourceRowHash = i.SourceRowHash
WHERE i.AlertTitle = %s
  AND i.Concept = 'Command_File_Mention' AND o.Concept = 'Command_File_Mention'
  AND i.GraphValue IN (%s)
ORDER BY o.AlertId, o.SourceRowHash, o.EntityIndex, o.GraphValue, i.GraphValue
LIMIT 501

SELECT DISTINCT o.AlertId, o.AlertTitle, o.ObservedAt, o.EntityIndex,
       o.GraphValue AS value, o.RawComponents, o.Roles, o.SourceRowHash,
       i.GraphValue AS matched_input
FROM LTMInputEvidence i
JOIN LTMEntityEvidence o ON o.SourceRowHash = i.SourceRowHash
WHERE i.AlertTitle = %s
  AND i.Concept = 'Command_File_Mention' AND o.Concept = 'Account_SID'
  AND i.GraphValue IN (%s,%s,%s,%s)
ORDER BY o.AlertId, o.SourceRowHash, o.EntityIndex, o.GraphValue, i.GraphValue
LIMIT 501

steps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.AlertId, o.AlertTitle, o.ObservedAt, o.EntityIndex,
       o.GraphValue AS value, o.RawComponents, o.Roles, o.SourceRowHash,
       i.GraphValue AS matched_input
FROM LTMInputEvidence i
JOIN LTMEntityEvidence o ON o.SourceRowHash = i.SourceRowHash
WHERE i.AlertTitle = %s
  AND i.Concept = 'File_Name' AND o.Concept = 'Command_File_Mention'
  AND i.GraphValue IN (%s)
ORDER BY o.AlertId, o.SourceRowHash, o.EntityIndex, o.GraphValue, i.GraphValue
LIMIT 501

SELECT DISTINCT o.AlertId, o.AlertTitle, o.ObservedAt, o.EntityIndex,
       o.GraphValue AS value, o.RawComponents, o.Roles, o.SourceRowHash,
       i.GraphValue AS matched_input
FROM LTMInputEvidence i
JOIN LTMEntityEvidence o ON o.SourceRowHash = i.SourceRowHash
WHERE i.AlertTitle = %s
  AND i.Concept = 'Command_File_Mention' AND o.Concept = 'Account_SID'
  AND i.GraphValue IN (%s,%s,%s,%s)
ORDER BY o.AlertId, o.SourceRowHash, o.EntityIndex, o.GraphValue, i.GraphValue
LIMIT 501
